The submission is clear and well organized, and its strongest assets are real: paying customers, a closed-loop service, and a credible founder-market fit. To strengthen it, the team should:

1. Make the financials internally consistent and transparent. The plan says four pilots generated $41,500 (about $10,400 each), yet the standard package is $18,000 and the lighter one is $9,500. Explain what the pilots actually included, what price they paid, and how pilot revenue converts to the stated pricing. Also reconcile year-one projections (12 schools, $190,000 implies about $15,800 per school) with the $18,000 average. Provide a simple table of assumptions (price mix, conversion rate, churn, coach capacity) rather than topline numbers only.

2. Replace 'profitable on paper' with real unit economics. Founders take no salary and advisors work free, so the 60% gross margin and profitability claims are flattering. Show fully loaded cost per school (coach hours per cycle, prep time, travel), what a market-rate coach salary does to margin, and how many schools one coach can serve. This directly tests whether the model scales beyond the founders' unpaid labor.

3. Address scalability and the human-delivery bottleneck. The key differentiator is a human coach sitting with teachers, which is hard to scale. Explain how the templates and dashboard reduce coach time, how coaches will be recruited, trained, and quality-controlled, and what the capacity ceiling is per coach. Part-time former teachers raise consistency and retention questions that should be addressed.

4. Provide evidence of impact, not just demand. The model hinges on renewals driven by demonstrated student growth, but the plan offers no results from the pilots. Include any before/after data on targeted standards, teacher testimonials, or a plan for rigorous measurement. Note the confounding factors and how impact will be credibly attributed. Name the pilot schools or quote them with permission, and state the renewal intent more concretely (two of four say they want to sign; are there letters of intent?).

5. Tighten the market sizing and go-to-market. The $63M TAM is a simple top-down multiplication (3,500 x $18,000) and assumes all target schools would buy at full price. Add a bottom-up serviceable market for the home state (about 140 schools), expected sales cycle length, budget sources (Title funds, grants), and who the actual buyer is. Explain how 12 schools next year will be acquired given 30-plus conversations so far, including the funnel and conversion rates.

6. Strengthen the competitive and defensibility discussion. Acknowledging that a bigger firm could copy the model is honest, but 'early relationships and templates' is thin. Discuss what is proprietary, how switching costs or data accumulation create a moat, and how the offering differs from existing instructional coaching and tutoring providers, which are not discussed. Consider also the risk of AI tools generating lesson plans from data cheaply.

7. Sharpen the ask and the use of funds. State the dollar amount sought and give a budget breakdown tied to milestones (for example, hiring two coaches at a given cost, dashboard development hours, conference costs) and what measurable outcomes the money will produce. Doubling customers is stated, but the link between spend and that result is not shown.

8. Address team and risk gaps. The team is all students or recent graduates with limited sales and operations experience, and it is unclear whether they will stay on full time after graduation. Clarify commitment, roles after hiring, and the plan for sales expertise. Add a brief risk section covering seasonality of the school calendar, charter funding volatility, student-data privacy and FERPA compliance (critical when handling student records), and dependence on a few early customers.

9. Polish the writing and presentation. Fix typos and informal phrasing ('alot', 'thru'), add the specific data source behind the 8,000 schools and charter statistics, and include one visual (a process diagram, financial table, or pilot case example) so the plan is easier to scan and more persuasive to judges.
